# Baselines and the fair-comparison protocol {#sec-baselines}

Every accuracy claim in this book compares ISLA against
GeoTransolver, and where stated against plain Transolver, under one protocol
that fixes everything except the architecture: matched sampled points per
case and epochs, each architecture at its own best learning rate, two or
more seeds, shared validation cases, and sealed test splits opened once. The
baselines are strong, not straw: GeoTransolver has at least as many
parameters as ISLA (9.0M against 8.9M) and receives raw coordinates that ISLA
never sees. On the recipe's compiled path at 10,000 tokens ISLA's training
step is 1.05x GeoTransolver's at half the peak memory (47 ms and 1.30 GiB
against 45 ms and 2.70 GiB; @sec-resource-matching). One item of the
protocol decides more than any architectural choice in this book: the scale
at which each model receives the freestream. Every architecture receives it
as a unit direction. Fed the physical freestream velocity instead
(2,679.5 in/s on HiLiftAeroML), GeoTransolver's global-context projector
collapses to one occupied slice and both baselines lose 3.4–3.8x at 35
training cases, so a comparison against a physical-velocity baseline
measures the input scale, not the architecture (@sec-part-baseline).
Two further questions are settled here so that the results chapters need not
carry them: ISLA's exact equivariance is *not* an accuracy advantage over a
canonicalized GeoTransolver (exactly pose-invariant at 1.01x cost), and
learning-rate choice belongs to the protocol because a shared rate would
have decided the comparison by tuning.

## The baselines and what each one sees {#sec-part-baseline}

**The comparison is against two members of the Transolver family: the same
soft-slice attention as ISLA, fed raw geometric inputs in place of ISLA's
invariants.** Transolver (Wu et al., ICML 2024, arXiv
[2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) is a transformer for physics
fields on unstructured point sets. Each layer assigns every point a softmax
mixture over a fixed number of *slices*, pools point features into one token
per slice, runs attention among the slice tokens, and scatters the result
back through the same mixture. ISLA (@sec-mt2) shares this backbone; it
differs in what enters the routing and what the tokens may carry.

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's reference surface model. Per surface point
it receives the coordinates (centered on the case) and the unit normal as a
six-channel feature; the freestream velocity vector is a three-channel global
feature. Its *geometry encoder* takes the coordinates a second time through a
dedicated embedding path that conditions the slice attention; the ball-query
local-feature path (`include_local_features`) is off throughout this program.
Twelve layers, hidden width 256, 256 slices, 9.0M parameters. It is not
rotation- or translation-equivariant: rotate the car and it sees a different
input.

::: {#sec-transolver}
**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder, the control
that isolates what the encoder contributes. Per point it receives coordinates
and normal; the freestream vector is broadcast to every point. Eight layers,
hidden 256, 256 slices, 6.0M parameters. On HiLiftAeroML, the only dataset
on which it is run in this book, it trains at learning rate 3e-3, its best
of the two rates run.
:::

**ISLA** receives position, unit normal and cell area per point and the unit
freestream direction as its only global input in this book's datasets,
consumed through invariants
and equivariant anchors only (@sec-mt2): 12 layers, hidden 192, 256 slices,
8.9M parameters.

**The numerical scale at which the freestream enters the baselines is a
protocol variable, and on HiLiftAeroML it moves their error more than any
architectural choice in this book.** ISLA consumes the unit freestream
direction by construction. GeoTransolver and Transolver consume whatever
vector the dataset pipeline hands them, and the pipelines pass the physical
freestream velocity through without normalizing: 2,679.5 in/s on
HiLiftAeroML (the dataset is in inches and seconds) and 38.9 m/s on
DrivAerML. Coordinates and fields are nondimensionalized; this one global
vector is not. GeoTransolver's global-context projector applies linear maps
and a slice softmax to it directly, and its conditioning depends on the
magnitude: with the production projector dimensions and untrained weights,
the entropy-equivalent number of occupied slices per head is 191–232 at
freestream magnitude 1, 1.0–3.8 at 38.9 and 1.00–1.02 at 2,679.5, while the maximum
context magnitude rises from 0.66 to 22.7 to 1,530
(results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json); Transolver
concatenates the raw vector into every point's features. Training can in
principle rescale either path, so the conditioning numbers are the
initialization signature of the hazard; the trained measurement is what
counts.

The trained measurement, at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases with the same
cases, seeds, budget and learning rates in both arms (GeoTransolver 1e-3,
Transolver 3e-3): surface-pressure relative L2 on the 180 shared validation
cases is 0.124 for GeoTransolver fed the unit direction against 0.381 fed
the physical velocity (three seeds 0.374, 0.409, 0.359), and 0.115 for
Transolver against 0.404. Each unit-direction baseline is lower than its
physical-velocity twin on 180 of 180 cases, by a median factor of 3.4
(GeoTransolver) and 3.8 (Transolver); velocity and wall shear move the same
way (GeoTransolver 0.145 and 0.229 against ISLA's 0.168 and 0.256,
Transolver 0.140 and 0.216;
results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json; @sec-nb-udrv-verdict). At its best
learning rate (3e-3 at this rung) the unit-direction GeoTransolver reaches 0.111.
Against ISLA's reference configuration (0.1529) and its constant-gauge
variant (0.1377) the unit-direction baselines are ahead: GeoTransolver 0.73x and
0.80x, Transolver 0.75x and 0.83x, and GeoTransolver at 1e-3 is lower than
the constant-gauge variant on 130 of 180 cases, Transolver on 152
(@sec-de-result). The 3.4–3.8x factor is a statement about what
GeoTransolver and Transolver do when fed a vector of magnitude 2,679.5 at
small data, and nothing else; at 1,260 cases the physical-velocity GeoTransolver
reaches parity with ISLA regardless (@sec-data-efficiency).

Three rules follow. First, every architecture receives the freestream as a
unit direction, and a comparison against a baseline fed the physical
velocity is reported as a measurement of the input scale, never as a
comparison of architectures. Second, the unit-direction baseline is the
reference baseline on every rung; the 35-, 210- and 510-case rungs, the 4-
and 21-geometry rungs and the fixed-angle split each have one, and the
1,260-case rung does not yet (@sec-data-efficiency, @sec-program-status).
Third, the protocol fixes the input scale by rule rather than by control:
learning-rate, training-length and seed controls vary the optimizer and
cannot detect an input-scale defect, and neither can appending invariant
features to the baselines' inputs (@sec-mechanism). On DrivAerML the hazard
is smaller and its trained effect is nil: at 38.9 m/s the projector's collapse
at initialization is partial, and GeoTransolver trained on the physical
velocity scores 0.0498 against 0.0503 on the unit direction at 435 cars
(float32; @sec-full-data). GeoTransolver's volume configuration on the
interior task changes by under 2% on every field between the two freestream
inputs, so
the interior ordering is not an input-scale effect (@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict).

| architecture | per-point inputs | global input | layers | hidden | slices | parameters | peak memory at 10k tokens |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GeoTransolver | centered coordinates, unit normal; coordinates again through the geometry encoder | freestream vector, consumed by the global-context projector: the unit direction under the protocol (the physical velocity is the hazard measured above) | 12 | 256 | 256 | 9.0M | 2.70 GiB |
| Transolver | centered coordinates, unit normal | freestream vector, broadcast per point: the unit direction under the protocol | 8 | 256 | 256 | 6.0M | not measured |
| ISLA | position, unit normal, cell area (via invariants and anchors only) | unit freestream direction | 12 | 192 | 256 | 8.9M | 1.30 GiB with the geometry recompute; 1.94 GiB without |

: The three architectures compared on the aerodynamic datasets. *Per-point
inputs*: channels attached to each of the 10,000 sampled surface points per
case. *Global input*: the one per-case vector. *Layers*: soft-slice attention
blocks in the encoder. *Hidden*: width of the per-point feature vector.
*Slices*: slice tokens per layer. *Parameters*: trainable parameters of the
recipe configuration. *Peak memory*: peak allocated GPU memory over one
training step on one case of 10,000 sampled points in bfloat16 on one GB300,
both models compiled as the recipe runs them, the same harness for both
(results/kernel_study_2026-09-13/pareto_gb300_full_bf16.json; @sec-mt2-cost).
Not measured for Transolver, which serves only as a same-family control on
HiLiftAeroML. Configuration source:
`unified_external_aero_recipe/conf/model/{isla_surface,geotransolver_surface,transolver_surface}.yaml`
(`isla_surface_constant_gauge.yaml` pins the constant-gauge variant; before
2026-09-15 the two ISLA files were named `isla_surface_reference.yaml` and
`isla_surface.yaml`).
{#tbl-architectures}

## The fair-comparison protocol {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in this book was produced under the
following protocol; a comparison that violates any item is not reported.**
Datasets and splits are defined in @sec-problem, the metric in @sec-metrics.

1. **Matched tokens per case: 10,000 sampled surface points for every
   architecture.** Accuracy still rises with tokens at 10,000 (6,500 to
   10,000 is worth 8% for ISLA, @sec-resource-matching), so a token mismatch
   would be a handicap disguised as an architecture difference.
2. **Matched epochs: 500 for every arm, one case per step.** A short budget
   favours the faster starter; the 1,000-epoch GeoTransolver controls at 35
   and 210 training cases (@sec-data-efficiency) do not lower its error, so
   500 does not under-train the baseline. Under the recipe's
   step schedule (@sec-protocol) the second 500 epochs are a low-rate tail,
   not a doubled optimization budget.
3. **Learning rate chosen per architecture on the full split, by
   validation, before any ladder or ablation ran.** From the grid
   {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2} on DrivAerML and {1e-3, 3e-3} on HiLiftAeroML: ISLA 1e-3
   on both datasets; GeoTransolver 1e-3 on HiLiftAeroML and 3e-3 on
   DrivAerML; each then frozen for every smaller split and ablation. The one
   departure is disclosed where it occurs: Transolver had no full-split run
   on HiLiftAeroML, so it was trained at both 1e-3 and 3e-3 on the 35- and
   210-case rungs and is reported at the better of the two per rung (3e-3 at
   both), a choice that favours the baseline (@sec-data-efficiency). Choosing after seeing
   ladder results would let the tuning budget set the gap (@sec-lr-protocol).
4. **Every architecture receives the freestream as the unit direction**,
   and, on a dataset whose speed varies between cases, a separately
   normalized speed channel alongside it. The dataset pipelines do not
   nondimensionalize global inputs, and a raw physical velocity of
   2,679.5 in/s costs GeoTransolver and Transolver 3.4–3.8x at 35
   HiLiftAeroML cases (@sec-part-baseline). A number produced with the
   physical velocity is labelled physical-velocity and is a measurement of the
   input scale, not a comparison of architectures.
5. **Two or more seeds per cell, reported individually.** Seed spread is
   the only noise estimate at 48 or 180 validation cases; every ratio is
   quoted with both seeds so the reader can see whether it exceeds the
   spread.
6. **Shared validation cases.** All architectures are scored on the same
   180 HiLiftAeroML cases or 48 DrivAerML cars, sampled with the same seed.
7. **Paired per-case statistics where a ratio is claimed.** A ratio of
   means can be carried by a few cases, so the count of validation cases on
   which one architecture is more accurate, with median and worst-decile
   per-case ratios, is reported alongside (@sec-data-efficiency).
8. **Sealed test splits evaluated once.** The 360-case HiLiftAeroML test
   set and the regime-extrapolation test lists (@sec-regime-extrapolation)
   are taken verbatim from the dataset manifest and evaluated a single time.
   "Sealed" is a per-checkpoint property (no model is scored on a case it
   trained on); it is not a program-level one, because the manifests overlap
   (@sec-splits) and the regime-extrapolation tests already read every
   geometry, so no later HiLiftAeroML test evaluation is an independent
   confirmation of the program's choices (@sec-limits-validation).
9. **Preregistered bars.** Each experiment states, in readout units and
   before it runs, the value that confirms and the value that refutes.

### One instrument per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

The *instrument* for a dataset is its fixed validation set and evaluation
configuration: on DrivAerML, surface pressure and wall shear on 48 held-out
cars at 10,000 sampled cells; on HiLiftAeroML, pressure, velocity, wall
shear, temperature and density on 180 held-out cases shared by every training
split. An instrument is never widened after a result is read from it; a
control that changes it (another token count, a rotated pose, a biased
sampling density) is reported as such, never mixed into an in-family number.
Its limits bind where stated: 48 cars is a small validation set and two seeds
a thin noise estimate (@sec-limits).

## Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**At the recipe operating point ISLA matches GeoTransolver on parameters
and tokens per case, and on the compiled path it matches on step time at
half the memory.** Parameters 8.9M against 9.0M; tokens per case 10,000
each. On one GB300 in bfloat16 at batch 1, both models compiled as the
recipe runs them (results/kernel_study_2026-09-13/pareto_gb300_full_bf16.json;
@sec-mt2-cost), GeoTransolver steps in 45 ms at 2.70 GiB of peak memory.
ISLA steps in 47 ms at 1.30 GiB with its geometry recompute on (1.05x) and
in 39 ms at 1.94 GiB without it (0.86x); the two paths are bitwise
identical in output and gradients. At 40,000 tokens the default compiled
ISLA takes 119 ms against GeoTransolver's 53 ms (2.2x), and the exact fused
geometry kernel (opt-in, `geo_kernel="fused"`) takes 52 ms at 4.5 GiB
against 10.0 GiB. Every stage but the MLP is memory-bound, and the relational
invariants carry 61% of the traffic (@sec-nb-kernel-study). Memory was not a
controlled variable in any comparison: the checkpoints in this book were
trained by an implementation of the same function (float64 agreement 4e-15)
with a larger footprint, so no accuracy result depends on the footprint.

@tbl-token-control is a token-count control, not a matched-memory one. It
reports DrivAerML validation pressure error, relative L2 per car averaged
over 48 cars, at the frozen rate 3e-3 for both architectures (not ISLA's best
rate; the comparison of interest is ISLA against ISLA), for ISLA's
constant-gauge variant. Cutting ISLA's tokens from 10,000 to 6,500 costs 8%
accuracy. The 8% is the price of fewer sampled points per case, which is
why the protocol fixes tokens at 10,000 for every architecture; it is not
evidence about memory.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-token-control
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path

R = Path("..") / "results"
iw = json.load(open(R / "instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json"))
p = lambda k: iw[k]["pressure_l2"]
# artifact keys: "ref_mt2_v3c" is ISLA's constant-gauge variant at lr 3e-3
mt2_const_10k = [p(f"ref_mt2_v3c_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
mt2_const_6500 = [p(f"iw_mt2_v3c_r6500_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
gt_10k = [p(f"ref_gt_fixed_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
mean = lambda v: sum(v) / len(v)
ratio = mean(mt2_const_6500) / mean(mt2_const_10k)
rows = [
    ("ISLA, constant-gauge variant", "10,000", mt2_const_10k, 1.0),
    ("ISLA, constant-gauge variant", "6,500", mt2_const_6500, ratio),
    ("GeoTransolver", "10,000", gt_10k, None),
]
out = "| architecture | tokens per case | pressure rel-L2 (seed 42 / 43) | relative to ISLA at 10,000 |\n|---|--:|---|--:|\n"
for n, t, v, r in rows:
    rr = "--" if r is None else f"{r:.2f}x"
    out += f"| {n} | {t} | {v[0]:.4f} / {v[1]:.4f} | {rr} |\n"
print(out)
print(": The token-count control on DrivAerML. *Tokens per case*: sampled "
      "surface cells per car in training and validation. "
      "*Pressure rel-L2*: relative L2 error of surface pressure per car, "
      "mean over the 48 validation cars, scored in bfloat16, at learning "
      "rate 3e-3 for every row (not ISLA's best rate); the ISLA rows are the "
      "constant-gauge variant. The last column divides the row's seed mean by "
      "that of ISLA at 10,000 tokens. This is a token-count control, not a "
      "matched-memory one. Not "
      "shown: wall shear, which moves the same way. Data: "
      "results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json.")
```

## Pose: equivariant by construction, invariant by canonicalization {#sec-pose}

**ISLA is rotation- and translation-covariant by algebraic construction
(exact in float64; the bf16 training path carries a finite-precision
residual that is measured, not assumed, @sec-mt2-contracts);
GeoTransolver trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at 1.01x
accuracy cost. Against a canonicalized baseline the two are equally good, so
equivariance is a contract about what the model needs at inference, not an
accuracy advantage. Against baselines that learn pose from SO(3)
augmentation instead, ISLA leads by 6% (GeoTransolver) and 19% (Transolver)
when every DrivAerML car arrives in a random pose (@sec-scoreboard-pose).**

The two phrases mean different things. A model is *equivariant by
construction* when every operation inside it commutes with rigid motions: its
inputs are invariants or vectors in an equivariant basis, so a rotated case
yields the rotated prediction to floating-point roundoff (ISLA's fp64 contract
test, @sec-mt2). A pipeline is *invariant by canonicalization* when a
preprocessing step estimates a frame from each case, expresses the case in
that frame, runs an ordinary non-equivariant model, and rotates vector outputs
back; it is invariant exactly when the frame estimate depends on the
pose-free geometry alone.

The canonical frame used here sends the freestream direction to +x and fixes
the roll about it from the area-weighted principal axes of the surface in the
transverse plane, sign from the third moment. On DrivAerML no case is within
5% of a principal-axis degeneracy and the sign is consistent across all 48
validation cars. Estimated from the 10,000 sampled cells the model sees, the
frame is tilted 0.8° on average from the full-resolution frame (key `frame`
of the artifact cited in @tbl-pose).

@tbl-pose reports DrivAerML validation pressure error, relative L2 per car
averaged over 48 cars, for GeoTransolver at learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs,
two seeds, evaluated *in pose* (cars as the dataset provides them) and on an
*SO(3) orbit* (each car in a uniformly random orientation, rotation angles
44–179°), vector outputs rotated back before scoring.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pose
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path

R = Path("..") / "results"
p1 = json.load(open(R / "p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json"))
pp = json.load(open(R / "p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json"))
raw_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
raw_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_in = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["inpose_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_orb = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["orbit_SO3_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
mean = lambda v: sum(v) / len(v)
ref = mean(raw_in)
orbit_ratios = [v / p1["prior"]["gt_inpose_pressure_l2"]
                for v in p1["prior"]["gt_p1_orbit_pressure_l2"].values()]
fx = lambda r: f"{r:.0f}x" if r >= 10 else f"{r:.2f}x"
def row(name, a, b):
    return (f"| {name} | {a[0]:.4f} / {a[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(a)/ref)}) "
            f"| {b[0]:.4f} / {b[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(b)/ref)}) |\n")
out = "| GeoTransolver variant | in pose (seed 42 / 43) | SO(3) orbit (seed 42 / 43) |\n|---|---|---|\n"
out += row("trained and evaluated in the recipe frame", raw_in, raw_orb)
out += row("trained in the recipe frame, canonicalized at inference only", eval_canon_in, eval_canon_orb)
out += row("trained and evaluated in the canonical frame", tr_in, tr_orb)
print(out)
print(f": Pose dependence of GeoTransolver on DrivAerML. *In pose*: the 48 "
      f"validation cars in the orientation the dataset provides. *SO(3) "
      f"orbit*: the same cars, each in a uniformly random orientation. Cells "
      f"are surface-pressure relative L2 averaged over the 48 cars, seed 42 / "
      f"seed 43; the parenthesized factor divides the seed mean by the "
      f"in-pose seed mean of the first row ({ref:.4f}). Across three seeds "
      f"of the recipe-frame model the orbit penalty spans "
      f"{min(orbit_ratios):.0f}–{max(orbit_ratios):.0f}x. Not shown: ISLA, "
      f"whose orbit and in-pose predictions agree to fp64 roundoff by "
      f"construction; wall shear behaves the same way. Data: "
      f"results/p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json (rows 1–2), "
      f"results/p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json (row 3).")
```

Three things follow. First, GeoTransolver in the recipe frame is not
pose-robust: a random orientation takes it to 26–32x its in-pose error.
Second, canonicalization must be in the training pipeline. Applied only at
inference to a model trained in one exact pose it is pose-invariant but costs
1.6–1.7x, because that model is hypersensitive to sub-degree frame tilt (a
fixed 1° roll costs it 1.7–1.8x, 5° costs 6.5–6.8x; key `stage3` of the same
artifact) and the frame estimate carries about 0.8° of it; a model that sees
the estimator's tilt noise during training learns to ignore it, and the
penalty falls to 1.01x (row 3 of @tbl-pose). Third, on
this data ISLA's exact equivariance and canonicalized GeoTransolver deliver
the same pose invariance, so no accuracy claim in this book is attributed to
equivariance; the pose contract is scored as a contract.

What the contract still buys is generality. Canonicalization needs a known
freestream direction at inference and a principal frame whose sign can be
resolved; both hold for every vehicle and wing dataset here. They fail for a
PDE surrogate with no distinguished global direction, for bodies whose
transverse inertia tensor is degenerate or whose third moment vanishes (a
symmetry the estimator cannot break), and for assemblies of parts in mixed
orientations, where no single frame canonicalizes every component. ISLA needs
neither a frame estimate nor a freestream at inference; there the contract
is the difference between a working surrogate and a 26–32x failure.

## Learning-rate sensitivity is part of the protocol {#sec-lr-protocol}

**The two architectures lose very different amounts of accuracy at a wrong
learning rate: one grid step above its best, GeoTransolver degrades 4–14x on
DrivAerML and 6.5x on HiLiftAeroML where ISLA degrades 1.55x and 1.14x, so a
protocol sharing one rate would measure tuning luck instead of
architecture.** The quantity is validation pressure error, relative L2 per
case averaged over the validation cases, at 500 epochs and 10,000 tokens,
for every rate run on the full splits: on DrivAerML (435 training cars, 48
validation) the grid {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2}, two seeds per rung; on HiLiftAeroML
(1,260 training cases, 180 validation) the grid {1e-3, 3e-3}, two seeds per
rung. The full grid is plotted and reported as a robustness result in
@sec-robustness-lr (@fig-lr-robustness); here the point is procedural.

The grids are scored in bfloat16 and the ISLA arm is the constant-gauge
variant; the within-architecture degradation factors are what this section
uses. On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver's best rate is 3e-3 (0.0532) and at 1e-2
it degrades 4–14x (0.221 and 0.739 on the two seeds); ISLA's best is 1e-3
(0.0577) and at 1e-2 it degrades 1.55x (0.0874 and 0.0914). On HiLiftAeroML
both are best at 1e-3; at 3e-3 GeoTransolver destabilizes to 0.148 and
0.397, a 6.5x degradation of the seed mean, while ISLA moves from
0.040/0.043 to 0.045/0.049, a 1.14x degradation, so its four grid points
across both rates and both seeds span
0.040–0.049^[`results/highlift_wave_reduction.json`]. The HiLiftAeroML grid
fed GeoTransolver the physical velocity (@sec-part-baseline); its instability
at the higher rate with the unit direction is not yet measured
(@sec-program-status), so that figure is a physical-velocity measurement.

Two consequences are built into the protocol. First, because GeoTransolver's
best rate differs between datasets (3e-3 on DrivAerML, 1e-3 on HiLiftAeroML),
"best rate per architecture, chosen on the full split" is the only rule under
which the GeoTransolver baseline is the strongest version of itself on both.
The rate choice moves GeoTransolver's DrivAerML error by 3% between 1e-3
and 3e-3 (0.0548 against 0.0532, bfloat16) and does not decide the
comparison; the float32 standing under the best-rate rule is GeoTransolver
0.0503 against ISLA's reference configuration 0.0552 (@sec-full-data).
Second, the rate is chosen once and frozen for every smaller split: retuning
at 35 or 210 training cases would hand the baseline search that ISLA did not
get. Rate, training-length and seed controls at the small splits
(@sec-data-efficiency) move GeoTransolver's error by far less than its
input-scale sensitivity, which is why the input scale is fixed by rule and
not tested by control (@sec-part-baseline).
